Earnings Whisper

Estimate revisions ahead of a company's earnings release offer clues to the business conditions for the period whose results are coming out. This insight is at the core of our proprietary surprise prediction model -- the Zacks Earnings ESP (Expected Surprise Prediction).

The Zacks Earnings ESP compares the Most Accurate Estimate to the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the quarter; the Most Accurate Estimate is a more recent version of the Zacks Consensus EPS estimate. The idea here is that analysts revising their estimates right before an earnings release have the latest information, which could potentially be more accurate than what they and others contributing to the consensus had predicted earlier.

Thus, a positive or negative Earnings ESP reading theoretically indicates the likely deviation of the actual earnings from the consensus estimate. However, the model's predictive power is significant for positive ESP readings only.

Investing.com -- StoneX analyst Mark Zgutowicz downgraded Spotify to Hold from Buy in a new note to clients, citing limited catalysts for revenue per user over the next year alongside rising payments to record labels.

The shares are down 0.8% premarket on Thursday.

Zgutowicz told investors that he remains strongly convinced of Spotify's long-term network effects but sees difficult financial optics over the coming 12 months.

He pointed to ongoing step-ups in per-subscriber minimums with major labels, which raise royalty costs on plans where those minimums bind, including discounted plans.

Unsure what to buy ahead of earnings? Our AI's recent pre-earnings calls delivered gains of +77% to +118% after results dropped. See this month's earnings picks »

"We believe PSMs implemented over the past couple years have largely been shielded by Spotify's premium price increases, the last of which anniversaries in Jan. '27," Zgutowicz wrote. "Absent another broad premium price increase in CY27 –noting already three increases in the last three years– we expect less gross-margin expansion in '27E than consensus anticipates."

On product catalysts, the analyst said Spotify's AI Remix remains a work in progress, lacking full major label participation. Spotify has agreements with Universal Music Group, Merlin and Kobalt, but Warner Music and Sony remain holdouts.

"We doubt it would generate meaningful paid uptake without at least one more major and therefore would not underwrite a scaled rollout before mid-'27E," he said, adding that paid AI covers and remixes could strengthen the labels' negotiating hand.

StoneX trimmed its third-quarter revenue estimate to 4.98 billion euros, slightly below guidance of about 5 billion euros. It cut its fourth-quarter and 2027 premium gross margin forecasts by 40 and 30 basis points, to 35.4% and 35.3%.

title: Is Spotify (SPOT) a Good or Bad Investment at Today’s Price?
detail:
Is Spotify (SPOT) a Good or Bad Investment at Today’s Price?
Suraj Santlani

SPOT
SPY
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Spotify Technology S.A. (NYSE:SPOT) closed at $527.45 on October 13. The stock has returned 4.6% over the last six months, compared to a 21.5% return by the Insider Monkey Billionaire Index and 14.0% for State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust.

Spotify sells access to music it does not own. Every song someone plays sends a royalty to the record label that holds the rights, and the labels negotiate what that royalty is. That single arrangement decides how much of your subscription Spotify is ever allowed to keep.

READ ALSO: 10 High Growth S&P 500 Stocks to Buy Now

Is Spotify (SPOT) a Good or Bad Investment at Today's Price?
People Do Not Cancel Music:

Music is a habit rather than a purchase. Once someone has built playlists and followed artists on one service, moving to another means starting again, and most people never bother. That is why Spotify keeps the customers it wins.

It is also still growing. Revenue rose 13.90% in the most recent quarter, which is quick for a company already this large, and most new subscribers arrive without Spotify paying much to find them.

The balance sheet is the strongest part of the case. Spotify holds about $7 billion in cash against a few hundred million of debt, so it pays for its own growth and owes almost nothing to anyone. That profile is what we were looking for in the names we backed for high returns this year, where the one we ranked first is up 24% since January.

The Labels Set the Ceiling:

Gross margin is 32.77%, which means most of every subscription dollar leaves as a royalty before Spotify pays a single employee. Raising the price does not fix that, because the labels are paid a share of revenue and their share goes up too.

So the growth arrives at a profit margin Spotify cannot improve. Adding subscribers makes the company bigger without making each subscriber much more valuable, which is what separates it from the growth stocks Dan Loeb has been adding. The one he holds most of is up 9% since.

The Valuation Case:

Spotify trades at 28.57 times next year's expected earnings, against 27.98 times what it earned last year, on analyst consensus estimates. A forward figure above a trailing one is unusual, and it means analysts expect the company to earn less next year than it just did.

A price near 30 times earnings is normally reserved for companies expected to grow profits quickly, and this one is expected to do the opposite, making the valuation hard to justify. The verdict is that Spotify looks expensive for what the business is currently set up to deliver, and the cash pile is most of what holds the case together.
